# 1 Enoch Chapter 101 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## 101:1 — 'children of heaven' address

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "ye-children-of-heaven" | Literal; archaic 'ye' |
| LOGOS | "you children of heaven" | Formal |
| PNEUMA | "you children of heaven" | Agrees with LOGOS |

**SOPHIA:** Adopted LOGOS/PNEUMA 'you children of heaven.' All agree on substance. The address 'children of heaven' may mean the righteous, the angels, or humanity in general — the ambiguity is preserved.

---

## 101:3 — 'petition' vs. 'pray your way out'

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "ye-cannot-petition-Him" | Literal; legal-petitionary language |
| LOGOS | "you cannot petition Him" | Formal |
| PNEUMA | "you won't be able to pray your way out of it" | Colloquial; 'pray your way out' is interpretive |

**SOPHIA:** Adopted LOGOS 'petition.' The Ge'ez uses a term for formal petition or request — the legal register is important and should be preserved.

---

## 101:4 — 'in sore trouble' vs. 'in great distress'

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "are-in-sore-trouble" | Archaic |
| LOGOS | "are in great distress" | Formal; modern equivalent |
| PNEUMA | "how desperate their situation becomes" | Paraphrase; focuses on the situation not the state |

**SOPHIA:** Adopted LOGOS 'in great distress.' 'Sore trouble' (EMET) is archaic. PNEUMA's 'desperate situation' redirects from the emotional state (distress) to the circumstances.

---

## 101:5 — 'evil foreboding of heart'

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "evil-forebodings-of-heart" | Literal compound |
| LOGOS | "evil foreboding of heart" | Formal |
| PNEUMA | "dread in their hearts" | 'Dread' for 'evil foreboding'; restructured |

**SOPHIA:** Adopted LOGOS 'evil foreboding of heart.' The Ge'ez compound 'evil-of-heart' idiom is significant; 'foreboding' captures the anticipatory nature of the fear. PNEUMA's 'dread' is simpler but loses the specific forward-looking quality.

---

## 101:7 — Sea personification: 'afraid and dries up'

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "at-His-rebuke-it-is-afraid-and-dries-up" | Literal personification |
| LOGOS | "at His rebuke it is afraid and dries up" | Formal; preserves personification |
| PNEUMA | "At his rebuke, the sea shrivels and dries up" | 'Shrivels' for 'is afraid'; loses personification |

**SOPHIA:** Adopted LOGOS. 'Afraid' (is afraid) is the correct rendering — the sea is personified as experiencing fear. PNEUMA's 'shrivels' drops the personification in favor of a physical description.

---

## 101:9 — Final antithesis: sailors vs. sinners

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "Do-not-the-sailors-of-the-ships-fear-the-sea? Yet-sinners-fear-not-the-Most-High." | Literal; antithetical chiasm |
| LOGOS | "Do not the sailors of the ships fear the sea? Yet sinners fear not the Most High." | Formal; preserves rhetorical structure |
| PNEUMA | "Sailors fear the sea. But sinners don't fear the Most High." | Compressed; loses interrogative |

**SOPHIA:** Adopted LOGOS. The rhetorical question ('Do not the sailors...?') is part of the original structure — it invites agreement before the devastating contrast. PNEUMA's declarative compression is effective but alters the rhetorical move.

---

**Total disagreements this chapter: 5**
